title: Is the Last Layer Sufficient for Uncertainty Quantification?
claim: Restricting linearization to the final layer leaves the predictive uncertainty estimates essentially unchanged relative to full-network linearization.
layout: 2x2 grid of heatmaps, rows are datasets, columns are methods, shared colorbars
description: A 2x2 grid of heatmaps. Columns are labeled DNN-GLM (full-network linearization) on the left and LL-GLM (last-layer linearization) on the right. The top row is the Three Islands dataset, with three clusters of points in pink, dark blue and yellow. The bottom row is the Two Moons dataset, with interleaved dark-blue and yellow crescents. Each panel's background shows the variance of the maximum softmax probability, using a plasma colormap from dark purple (0) to bright yellow (1). Uncertainty is low (dark) near the data and high (yellow) far from it. The left and right panels in each row look almost the same, which shows that the last-layer approximation preserves UQ quality. Each row has a vertical axis label and a colorbar on its right. The eye goes first to the bright, high-contrast scatter clusters.
caption: Variance of the maximum softmax probability, on the (top) Three Islands dataset and (bottom) Two Moons dataset. We see that a last-layer approximation does not affect quality of UQ. Excerpt from [ref].
abstract: Epistemic uncertainty quantification (UQ) for deep neural networks (DNNs) is a requirement for safe adoption of AI in mission-critical settings. Several leading methods for UQ linearize DNNs to form Bayesian Generalized Linear Models (GLMs), where epistemic uncertainty is modeled via the predictive posterior distribution. Linearizing around the parameters of the final connected layer of a DNN is a commonly used approximation for reducing the computational burden of such GLMs, though it is often believed to come at the cost of degraded performance. In this work, we compare GLMs arising from full-network and last-layer linearization using both theoretical and empirical approaches. We first employ tools from random matrix theory to conduct a theoretical comparison; this analysis reveals no meaningful improvement in the UQ capabilities of full linearization. Coupled with a large-scale empirical evaluation across a range of modern machine learning tasks, we arrive at the following conclusion: a last-layer approximation yields comparable UQ performance while offering substantially improved computational efficiency.
